title: n8n, Zapier, or Make: which one fits and why
promise: You'll know which of the three suits the process you wrote in the previous lesson. You'll leave the reason written in one line. And you'll know the exact signal that'll warn you the day you need to switch.
why: Alvaro builds automations for three dental clinics. He started on Zapier because that's what showed up in the videos, and it worked: appointment reminders, patient sign-ups, alerts to the dentist. The problem arrived with the fourth clinic. Every reminder is four tasks, and each clinic sends two hundred a month. The bill went from $20 to $180 without him changing anything. That month he discovered he'd spent a year paying for something that on n8n would have been a loop (repeating the same steps for each appointment) at no cost. It's not that Zapier was a bad choice: it's that it stopped being one and nobody warned him.

theory.title: All three do the same thing, then stop doing it
theory.text: For a four-step process between two well-known applications, all three work and the difference is almost a matter of taste. Zapier is the simplest and has the most integrations, meaning ready-made connections with other applications. Make is the best at showing the data's journey, with its bubble canvas. n8n is the one that holds up under real logic and the only one you can install on your own server. The choice only matters once the process grows.
theory.analogy: Any of the three cars works for a grocery run. The difference shows up the day you have to move house.

visual.title: All three, side by side
visual.caption: For four steps between two apps, all three work. The difference shows up as the process grows.

theory.title: The price gets charged on different things, and that's the trap
theory.text: Zapier and Make charge per task run: every completed action adds up. That's cheap while volume is low and spikes as it grows, especially with processes that go through lists. n8n's cloud charges per flow execution, not per step. A twenty-step flow costs the same as a two-step one. And self-hosted on your own server, there's no license cost: you only pay for the server itself.
theory.example: A flow that processes 500 rows, calling an API (the door through which one program requests data from another) for each one: on Zapier that's 500 tasks. On n8n it's one execution.

visual.caption: A 4-action flow. What changes isn't the work: it's how each one counts it.

theory.title: The signal to switch isn't the price, it's the shape of the problem
theory.text: There are three clear signs you've outgrown Zapier or Make. The first: you need to repeat something for every item in a list. The second: the bill is growing faster than the work it's saving you. The third: the data passing through can't leave your company. With just one of the three, it's time to look at n8n; with two, don't think twice.
theory.analogy: You don't switch cars because the other one is prettier. You switch the day what you need to haul doesn't fit.

visual.title: The three signs you've outgrown it
visual.caption: One alone means it's time to look at n8n. Two, don't think twice.
visual.question: Which of these three describes your case right now?

branches.answer: I need to repeat something for every item in a list
branches.why: On Zapier and Make, every item in the list counts. A flow going through 300 rows eats a month's plan in one afternoon, and no setting fixes that.
branches.cost: The savings show up from month one

branches.answer: The bill is growing faster than the work it saves me
branches.why: It's the classic trap: you start paying $20 and six months later you're at $180 without having changed anything. Nobody warns you: the bill climbs silently.
branches.cost: From $180/month to about $8 in server costs

branches.answer: The data can't leave my company
branches.why: If you handle health data, payroll, or a third party's customer data, this isn't a preference: it can be a legal requirement. And it decides before price does.
Zapier or Make suit you perfectly and you'll build faster. Switching later means rebuilding a flow, not rebuilding your work. Don't switch for sport.

theory.title: The cost nobody counts is yours
theory.text: n8n is cheaper in dollars and more expensive in hours: it has to be understood, and if you install it yourself, it has to be maintained. If you're automating for yourself and have time, it pays off very fast. If you're automating for a client who won't touch anything and wants it to just work without calling you, choose Zapier's cloud or n8n's cloud. It'll save you eleven-at-night phone calls. That math needs doing beforehand, not after.
theory.example: Alvaro switched to self-hosted n8n, meaning installed on his own server, and saved $170 a month. He also bought himself a problem: when the server goes down on a Sunday, he's the one who fixes it.

tasks.title: Count your process's real tasks
tasks.where: On the card from the previous lesson
tasks.action: Multiply your flow's number of actions by how many times it fires a month. That number is what Zapier or Make will bill you. Write it next to the card.
tasks.expect: A number. Under 750 tasks a month you fit into cheap plans; over 2,000 it starts to hurt.
tasks.stuck: If your flow goes through lists, also multiply by the list's average size. That's where everything spikes.

tasks.title: Answer the three signals
tasks.action: Answer yes or no: do I need to repeat something for every item in a list? Is the data passing through here sensitive (health, payroll, a third party's customer data)? Is volume going to grow this year? Count the yeses.
tasks.expect: Zero or one yes: Zapier or Make suit you perfectly. Two or three: n8n.
tasks.stuck: If you're unsure about the data question, ask yourself whether you'd mind that information sitting on a foreign company's server.

tasks.title: Decide who's maintaining this a year from now
tasks.action: Write the name of the person who'll fix it when it breaks. If it's you and you have time, self-hosted n8n is an option. If it's a client who won't touch anything, or if you don't want Sunday phone calls, choose the cloud, whether n8n's or the others'.
tasks.expect: A written name. It changes the decision more than any feature comparison.
tasks.stuck: If the answer is "nobody," pick the simplest cloud option that works, and document the flow from day one.

tasks.title: Write the decision and the exit signal
tasks.action: Two lines: "I'm going with ___ because ___" and "I'll switch the day ___." The second is the important one. Writing the exit signal today prevents the year Alvaro lost overpaying without noticing.
tasks.expect: Two sentences. The second with a number in it, not a feeling.
tasks.stuck: Exit signals that work: "when the bill exceeds $60 a month," "when I need to go through a list," "when a client with medical data comes on board."

tasks.title: Set a date for the review
tasks.action: Create an alert six months out that says "check whether this automation tool is still the right one" and link your card. Thirty seconds now. And it's the only thing that makes the exit signal useful instead of just staying on paper.
tasks.expect: A dated event on the calendar.
tasks.stuck: If you don't use a calendar, write it on the card itself with the date in big letters.

errors.message: I chose Zapier and the bill has spiked without changing anything
errors.means: Your volume has grown, or your flow goes through lists and every item counts as a task. It's the most common thing and happens to everyone.
errors.fix: Check your account's task breakdown to see which flow is eating them up. It's almost always just one. That's the candidate to move to n8n; the rest can stay where they are.

errors.message: I chose self-hosted n8n and it's been three days with nothing automated
errors.means: You're solving a server problem instead of the problem you started with. It's the classic trap of self-hosting too soon.
errors.fix: Stop. Build your flow on n8n's cloud, or even on n8n running on your laptop, check it works, and move the installation afterward. Flow first, infrastructure second.

errors.message: My client doesn't want their data leaving the country
errors.means: It's not a quirk: it can be a legal requirement depending on the sector, especially healthcare, banking, or public services.
errors.fix: This decides for you: self-hosted n8n on a server you control, or n8n's cloud with the right regional option. And put in writing where the data ends up, because you'll be asked.

matters: Writing today the number that'll tell you it's time to switch. Without that number written down, you overpay for months without noticing, which is exactly what happened to Alvaro.
Counting tasks while also counting the lists. That's where Zapier's and Make's bills spike, and where people always underestimate.
Deciding who maintains this before choosing. Self-hosting with nobody to maintain it is a deferred problem, not a saving.
If there's health data, payroll, or a third party's customer data, that decides for you before price does.
ignore: "Number of integrations" comparisons. All three have whatever you'll actually use. And for anything without a node (a ready-made piece for connecting to an application) there's the generic API call, covered in lesson 28.
Choosing based on what shows up in videos. What you see there is whoever's sponsoring, not what fits your case.
Trying to decide forever. Switching tools later means rebuilding a flow, not rebuilding your work. Choose what works now.
canDo: Any of the three handles a four-step process between well-known applications, and handles it well.
All three have a trial good enough to build your first flow without paying anything.
All three export what you've built, so none of them fully holds your work hostage.
n8n also does what the others don't: loops, chained logic, and staying inside your own server.
cantDo: None of them fixes a badly designed process. Choosing the right tool doesn't make up for a badly written card.
None of them warns you you've outgrown it: the bill climbs silently and you only see it if you look.
n8n doesn't maintain itself if you install it yourself. Updates, backups, and outages are yours.
Zapier and Make don't get cheaper the more volume you push through; their model is exactly the opposite.
words: The unit Zapier and Make bill by: each completed action. A four-step flow is four tasks per run.
The unit n8n's cloud bills by: every time the whole flow runs, whether it has two steps or twenty.
Installed on your own server. No license cost, and maintenance is on you.
On the vendor's servers, paying a fee. No maintenance, less control.
Repeating the same steps for every item in a list. It's what spikes the bill on some tools and not others.
The country where data is physically stored. Legally relevant in healthcare, banking, and the public sector.
next: With your decision written down, go to lesson 03: create the account or set up the installation, depending on what you chose, and get the environment ready to build the first flow.
